newsitem.title: IRAQ: Exodus to U.S. undermines Iraqi Kurd aid effort.
newsitem.headline: Exodus to U.S. undermines Iraqi Kurd aid effort.

text.p: Foreign aid workers, already struggling, say a U.S. evacuation of those involved in its relief effort may doom a five-year-old drive to rebuild northern Iraq.

Washington has flown around 1,300 Iraqis with ties to U.S.-funded aid organisations to the Pacific island of Guam via Turkey in the last four days. Another 3,000 are expected to leave this week in the face of Baghdad's increased influence in the mainly-Kurdish enclave.
"Suddenly the country has been stripped of its best people," said Peter Blackley of the British-based Save the Chidren Fund. "Those who left took a lot of expertise with them."
Other aid workers were more blunt. "The Americans have just ripped the guts out of the international effort here," said the manager of a European charity.

The latest exodus, aid workers said, touched off panic among Kurdish staff of all non-governmental organisations, fearful it portended a return to northern Iraq by the forces of President Saddam Hussein who has declared such aid work "illegal".

Iraq's Kurds have often fled their homes by the thousand to escape Baghdad's repression of Kurdish guerrillas. Iraq killed around 5,000 Kurdish civilians in a chemical weapons attack on the town of Halabja in 1988.

Western aid directors say they have been besieged in recent days by demands from Kurdish staff -- the vital drivers, translators and local experts -- for evacuation if their charities follow the U.S. example and pull out.
No other country has matched the American offer of asylum.

"We tell them that was never part of the deal, but of course you feel responsible all the same. Some people are genuinely terrified Saddam will return," said a mine disposal expert whose local teams were particularly concerned because of the military nature of their work.
"Everyone is asking, 'What do the Americans know that we don't?'" he said.
Morale is not much better among foreign nationals, who have dwindled in number as aid dollars dry up or logistical difficulties prove too much.

Veterans recount how the nightly "radio check" -- an electronic roll call by the U.N. radio room -- used to last 15 minutes as each expatriate called in. Now the evening ritual takes little more than five minutes.

Washington's latest evacuation of Kurds with aid groups receiving U.S. funding follows an earlier pull out of more than 2,000 who worked directly for the U.S. military and development mission in the north, carved from Baghdad's control by Western powers after the 1991 Gulf War.
The sudden announcement was the latest in a series of blows to the NGOs.

Rivalry between the two biggest Kurdish groups spilled into open warfare in August, when Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) forces used Baghdad's backing to attack its Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) rival.

The administrative centre of Arbil fell to the KDP-Iraqi assault. Sulaimaniya changed hands twice in as many weeks. The result was a tide of refugees, widespread looting and general lawlessness amid fears Saddam's troops were on their way.

Many local workers fled over the Iranian border, leaving the charities helpless. Most foreign staff pulled out or sought the safety of a U.S. compound in a hillside redoubt on the edge of Sulaimaniya.

New restrictions by the Turkish government have also begun to bite. Always wary of the NGO effort creating an independent "statelet" that might incite its own restive Kurdish minority, Ankara has not renewed permission for aid workers to use its Habur crossing point since August.
That has forced some aid workers to travel through Syria, a route ill-suited to the large scale imports the United Nations has authorised despite sanctions on Baghdad.
Leiv Christoffersen of Norwegian People's Aid, returned to Sulaimaniya after the latest troubles to assess prospects for restarting medical and demining work.
"Right now, I could not recommend that we start again," Christoffersen said.
